expertInsight: Salesforce is transitioning nonprofits from the legacy Nonprofit Success Pack (NPSP) managed package to the new Nonprofit Cloud, built natively on Data Cloud and Flow. NPSP implementations are still widely deployed and this exam remains active, but if you're starting a new nonprofit project or credential in 2026, check the Nonprofit Cloud certification page first, new engagements increasingly default to that architecture.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Nonprofit Success Pack Consultant Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The Nonprofit Success Pack Consultant exam is moderately difficult. It rewards practical Salesforce experience because many questions ask you to choose the best configuration, design, or troubleshooting approach rather than recall isolated definitions.
bullets: ~65% passing score: build a margin above the minimum before booking.
Scenario-based choices: expect questions that test when to use NPSP, Donations, or Households.
Hands-on context matters: candidates who have configured or supported Nonprofit Cloud and NPSP in a real org are better prepared than candidates who only memorize notes.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Aim for 75%+ on timed practice sets before booking. If your score is below that. Review the highest-weight topics first and retake questions until you can explain why each wrong option is wrong.

examFormat.heading: Nonprofit Success Pack Consultant Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The Nonprofit Success Pack Consultant exam is a timed Salesforce credential exam. Use the format below to plan pacing and practice-test strategy.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: A meaningful share of questions are scenario-based. The common pattern is a business requirement followed by several plausible Salesforce options; your job is to identify the safest, most maintainable choice for Nonprofit Cloud and NPSP.
bestWayToPass: Start with the official outline: Map each exam objective to your notes, Trailhead practice, and weak areas before taking full mocks.
Prioritize high-impact topics: Spend extra time on NPSP, Donations, and Households because these usually drive the hardest scenario questions.
Practice under time pressure: Use timed question sets so you learn when to move on and return to marked questions later.
Review explanations deeply: Do not just memorize the right option; write down why the other options are less appropriate for the scenario.

certificationCard.description: This exam focuses on configuring the NPSP managed package for nonprofits, covering household accounts, donation processing, recurring giving, customisable rollups, engagement plans, and data migration.

keyConcepts.h2: Nonprofit Success Pack Consultant: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: NPSP Installation and Configuration
blocks.body: NPSP is a managed package installed from **AppExchange**. The NPSP Settings page (in Setup or via the NPSP tile) controls all key configurations: Account model (Household vs Individual vs Organisation), relationship settings, payment behaviour, and rollup configuration. The Household Account model creates one Account per person (their household), not the same as a standard person account. The 1-to-1 Account model creates one Account per Contact. The consultant selects and documents the correct model before implementation and understands that switching models after data entry is complex.

blocks.heading: Donation Processing and Gift Entry
blocks.body: NPSP Batch Gift Entry enables high-volume gift processing with a grid-style interface optimised for data entry staff. Gift commitments (pledges with instalment schedules) are different from Recurring Donations (which auto-generate future Opportunities). Payment processing integrations (Stripe, PayPal, Elevate) handle online donations. The Gift Entry process typically includes: data entry, payment capture, acknowledgement letter generation, and tax receipt production. The consultant configures the Batch Gift Entry templates, defines required fields, and sets up payment matching rules.

blocks.heading: Customisable Rollups (CRLP)
blocks.body: Customisable Rollups (CRLP) replaces the legacy NPSP rollup system with a flexible, admin-configurable framework. Rollup types: Soft Credit rollups, Opportunity rollups to Contact/Account/GAU. Each rollup definition specifies: the source object and field, the rollup operation (SUM, COUNT, AVERAGE, FIRST/LAST DATE), filter criteria (e.g., only Closed Won Opportunities), and the target field on the Contact or Account. CRLP calculates totals like Total Given, Largest Gift, Most Recent Gift Date. The consultant configures CRLP to match the organisation's donor KPI requirements.

blocks.heading: Engagement Plans and Levels
blocks.body: Engagement Plans create task-based workflows for stewardship and donor cultivation. An Engagement Plan Template defines a sequence of tasks assigned to roles over time, e.g., 3 days after a major gift: send thank you note (task 1); 30 days: handwritten letter from ED (task 2); 60 days: phone call from program staff (task 3). Levels assign donors to stewardship tiers based on giving amounts: Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum. Level **Assignment rules** automatically categorise donors and can trigger Engagement Plans. The consultant configures Levels and Plans to match the organisation's major donor stewardship strategy.

blocks.heading: Data Quality and Migration
blocks.body: NPSP Data Importer is a tool specifically designed for importing constituent and donation data into NPSP, handling the household model logic, matching existing records, and creating correct relationships. It is preferred over Data Loader for initial NPSP data migration. Deduplication: NPSP includes merge tools for duplicate Contact and Account records. Data quality validation: using NPSP's built-in validation plus custom **Validation Rules** to enforce data completeness. The consultant designs the data migration strategy, mapping source system fields to NPSP objects, testing in sandbox, and validating results before production migration.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Nonprofit Success Pack Consultant Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The NPSP Consultant exam focuses specifically on configuring NPSP features for fundraising, constituent management, and reporting. The exam emphasizes practical configuration knowledge over architectural design.

blocks.heading: Recurring Donations Configuration
blocks.body: Know how to configure open-ended vs. fixed-length recurring donations, pause rules, and how recurring donation schedules generate Opportunities. Understand how Elevate (payment processor) integrates with recurring donations.

blocks.heading: Soft Credits & Household Rollups
blocks.body: Soft Credits track secondary donor credit (spouse, board member influence). Household Rollups aggregate giving totals at the household level. Know the rollup fields, their definitions, and how to customize them.

blocks.heading: Data Import Wizard for NPSP
blocks.body: Understand how to use the NPSP Data Import Wizard vs. standard Data Import Wizard for migrating constituent and gift data. Know field mappings and how to handle duplicate matching.

blocks.heading: Engagement Plans
blocks.body: Engagement Plans automate constituent stewardship tasks (thank-you calls, acknowledgment letters) triggered by donation milestones. Know how to configure Engagement Plan Templates and the task **assignment rules**.

blocks.heading: Reports & Dashboards for Nonprofits
blocks.body: Know key NPSP report types (NPSP Households, NPSP Soft Credits) and how to build fundraising dashboards tracking year-to-date giving, LYBUNT/SYBUNT donors, and retention rates.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Consultant Certifications
nextCertsAfter.intro: After this consultant certification, you can add adjacent clouds or deepen your specialisation:

sampleQuestions.question: In the Nonprofit Success Pack, what does a donation from an individual supporter normally look like?
options: A campaign member record created against the appeal the donation came from
A custom donation record created separately from the standard opportunity object
An opportunity linked to their household account
A payment record attached directly to the contact with no opportunity involved
sampleQuestions.explanation: NPSP uses the standard opportunity object for gifts, with the household account as the account on the record.
whyWrong: Campaign members record response, not the gift itself.
NPSP deliberately reuses opportunities rather than inventing a donation object.
Payments relate to an opportunity rather than replacing it.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the household account model?
options: It holds the grant applications the organisation has submitted this year
It records which volunteers are available for each of the upcoming events
It groups people who give and are addressed together
It stores the employer of each contact so that matching gifts can be claimed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Households let an organisation address a couple or family once and see their combined giving, which is how most individual fundraising works.
whyWrong: Grants are modelled as their own kind of opportunity.
Volunteer availability is tracked separately.
Employer relationships are handled by affiliations.

sampleQuestions.question: A supporter gives £20 every month by direct debit. How should this be set up?
options: As a single annual opportunity for £240 with a note describing the schedule
As a recurring donation that generates the instalments
As twelve separate opportunities created by hand at the start of each year
As a campaign with the supporter added as a member once every month
sampleQuestions.explanation: Recurring donations hold the schedule and generate the individual gift records, so the commitment and the instalments are both visible.
whyWrong: One annual figure hides whether each instalment was actually received.
Manual creation is laborious and breaks when the gift changes.
Campaign membership does not record money received.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a General Accounting Unit allocation do?
options: It stores the payment method the supporter used to make their gift
It records which member of the fundraising team secured the donation
It assigns part of a gift to a fund or purpose
It tracks the date on which the gift was acknowledged in writing
sampleQuestions.explanation: GAU allocations split a gift across funds or restricted purposes, which is what lets a nonprofit report on restricted income.
whyWrong: Payment method is a field on the payment record.
Credit to a fundraiser is handled by ownership and soft credits.
Acknowledgement is tracked by its own fields.

sampleQuestions.question: A couple gives jointly but only one of them is named on the cheque. How is the other recognised?
options: By creating a second opportunity for the same gift under their own name
Through a soft credit
By splitting the gift amount equally across two separate opportunities
By adding them as the primary contact and removing the original donor
sampleQuestions.explanation: Soft credits recognise influence or shared responsibility for a gift without double counting the income.
whyWrong: A duplicate opportunity inflates the organisation's reported income.
Splitting the amount understates what each person is associated with.
Replacing the donor misstates who actually gave.

sampleQuestions.question: Why does double counting matter so much in nonprofit reporting?
options: Duplicate records prevent acknowledgement letters from being generated
Reported income has to reconcile with the accounts
Soft credits are unable to be reported on alongside hard credit figures
Salesforce imposes a limit on how many opportunities an account may hold
sampleQuestions.explanation: Fundraising totals are published and audited, so a gift recorded twice overstates income and undermines trust in the data.
whyWrong: Letters can still be generated from duplicated records, wrongly.
Both can be reported on, which is precisely why the distinction is kept.
There is no such record limit in play.

sampleQuestions.question: An organisation receives a grant with reporting conditions attached. How is this usually handled?
options: As an opportunity with a record type for grants
As a recurring donation with the reporting dates set as its instalments
As a case raised against the funder so the conditions can be tracked
As a campaign with the funder added as the only member of that campaign
sampleQuestions.explanation: Grants are modelled as opportunities with their own record type and stages, which accommodates the application and reporting lifecycle.
whyWrong: A grant is not a regular recurring gift.
Cases are for service queries rather than income.
Campaigns group appeals and responses, not grant conditions.

sampleQuestions.question: What is batch gift entry used for?
options: Importing the organisation's entire contact database from a legacy system
Generating the acknowledgement letters for gifts received in the period
Reconciling the organisation's bank statement against its accounting system
Entering many gifts quickly and consistently
sampleQuestions.explanation: Batch gift entry gives a fast, validated screen for keying in a pile of gifts, which is what a post opening or event produces.
whyWrong: Bulk contact loading uses data import tools.
Acknowledgement is a separate downstream process.
Bank reconciliation happens in the finance system.

sampleQuestions.question: A supporter's spouse dies and the household should now reflect one person. What should the consultant consider?
options: Leaving the record unchanged so the giving history is not disturbed
Merging the two contact records so only one person remains in the system
Updating the household naming and salutation settings
Deleting the household account and attaching the survivor to a new one
sampleQuestions.explanation: Household names and salutations are generated from members, so they need updating to avoid addressing someone who has died.
whyWrong: Leaving it unchanged produces distressing correspondence.
Merging two people destroys one person's record entirely.
Deleting the household risks the giving history attached to it.

sampleQuestions.question: Why would an organisation use affiliations alongside the household model?
options: People relate to employers and other organisations too
Affiliations replace the need to record any soft credits on a gift
Affiliations are required before a recurring donation can be created
Household accounts are unable to hold more than two contacts each
sampleQuestions.explanation: A supporter may also be an employee, trustee or member of a partner organisation, and affiliations capture those links.
whyWrong: Affiliations and soft credits serve different purposes.
Recurring donations do not depend on affiliations.
Households can hold more than two members.

sampleQuestions.question: What should drive the design of an organisation's campaign hierarchy?
options: How the organisation actually plans and reports on appeals
The number of campaign records the Salesforce edition will permit
The preference of whichever fundraiser is most senior in the team
The order in which the campaigns were created in the legacy system
sampleQuestions.explanation: Campaigns exist to answer questions about appeal performance, so the hierarchy should mirror how the organisation plans and measures its fundraising.
whyWrong: Record limits are not the binding constraint on good design.
Seniority is not a design principle.
Legacy creation order rarely reflects current strategy.

sampleQuestions.question: A donor asks to stop receiving post but is happy with email. What does this require?
options: Channel-level preferences on the contact
Deletion of the donor's postal address from the household account record
Removal of the donor from every campaign in the organisation's database
A soft credit so the gift is still recorded without any contact being made
sampleQuestions.explanation: Consent and preference need to be recorded per channel, so mailings can exclude them while email continues.
whyWrong: Deleting the address loses information needed for gift aid and receipts.
Blanket campaign removal stops the email they do want.
Soft credits have nothing to do with contact preferences.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the risk of customising NPSP's standard objects heavily?
options: Salesforce removes support for the organisation's entire Nonprofit Cloud org
Future package upgrades become harder to absorb
The organisation loses the ability to report on any of its own donations
Recurring donations stop generating their scheduled instalment records
sampleQuestions.explanation: NPSP is a managed package that is updated regularly, so heavy divergence from its model makes each upgrade more work and more risk.
whyWrong: Support is not withdrawn for customisation.
Reporting continues to function on customised objects.
Recurring donations are not disabled by customisation as such.

sampleQuestions.question: An organisation wants to know its donor retention rate. What does this measure?
options: The number of new donors acquired during the current financial year
The total amount of income received compared with the previous year
The average size of the gifts received across the whole supporter base
The share of last year's donors who gave again
sampleQuestions.explanation: Retention asks how many existing donors came back, which is usually a cheaper source of income than acquiring new ones.
whyWrong: New donor counts measure acquisition rather than retention.
Total income can rise while retention falls.
Average gift size is a different measure entirely.

sampleQuestions.question: Which best describes what the Nonprofit Success Pack provides?
options: A finance and accounting system that replaces the organisation's ledger
A website builder for creating donation pages and supporter portals
A separate Salesforce product with its own entirely independent database
A fundraising data model built on standard Salesforce
sampleQuestions.explanation: NPSP is a managed package that adapts standard Salesforce objects to how nonprofits raise and report on money.
whyWrong: It is not a replacement for an accounting ledger.
Donation pages come from separate tools or Experience Cloud.
It runs on the same platform and objects, not a separate database.
